stem: An adult client has confirmed acute compartment syndrome of the lower leg. Which definitive treatment should the nurse anticipate?

options.A: Remove any restrictive cast or dressing and continue observation as the definitive treatment without operative decompression.
options.B: Urgent surgical fasciotomy with complete decompression of the affected compartments.
options.C: Elevate the extremity above heart level and delay operative treatment until swelling subsides.
options.D: Use analgesia and serial neurovascular examinations alone after the diagnosis is confirmed.

rationale: Acute compartment syndrome threatens tissue perfusion and is a surgical emergency. Current AAOS guidance on fasciotomy methods emphasizes that the essential operative goal is complete decompression of the affected compartments. StatPearls/NCBI likewise states that confirmed acute compartment syndrome requires immediate surgical management and fasciotomy to reduce intracompartmental pressure. Therefore B is correct. Removing a restrictive cast or dressing is an important initial measure but is not the definitive treatment once acute compartment syndrome is confirmed. Elevating the limb above heart level can reduce arterial inflow, and delaying decompression or relying only on analgesia/serial examinations risks irreversible ischemic injury.
educational_objective: Recognize confirmed acute compartment syndrome as a surgical emergency requiring urgent fasciotomy that completely decompresses the involved compartments; initial supportive measures do not replace definitive operative decompression.
source_organization: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS); NCBI Bookshelf / StatPearls
source_document_title: Management of Acute Compartment Syndrome Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline; Acute Compartment Syndrome
source_version_date: AAOS CPG adopted November 18, 2025; StatPearls last updated January 16, 2023 and carried in StatPearls 2026 edition; currentness live-rechecked August 16, 2026
source_locator: AAOS 2025 CPG, Summary/Fasciotomy Methods and Fasciotomy Methods section, printed pp.10 and 44: fasciotomy technique is less important than achieving complete decompression of the compartments of the affected extremity. StatPearls > Treatment/Management: acute compartment syndrome is an emergency; immediate surgical consultation, remove restrictive casts/dressings, keep extremity at heart level, and once diagnosis is confirmed immediate surgical fasciotomy is needed to reduce intracompartmental pressure.
source_claim_supported: Confirmed adult acute extremity compartment syndrome requires urgent operative fasciotomy with complete decompression; removing constricting devices and other supportive measures are initial adjuncts rather than substitutes for definitive decompression.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Physiological Adaptation, printed p.46: manage clients with acute or life-threatening physical health conditions; perform emergency care procedures; manage alteration in hemodynamics/tissue perfusion/hemostasis; recognize signs and symptoms of complications and intervene. Printed pp.48-49: Medical Emergencies and Pathophysiology content.

source_original.stem: A client is diagnosed with acute compartment syndrome of the lower leg. Which treatment should the nurse anticipate?

options.A: Observation with oral analgesics until swelling resolves.
options.C: Application of a tighter circumferential cast.
options.D: Vigorous massage of the affected extremity.

source_original.rationale: Acute compartment syndrome is a surgical emergency because rising compartment pressure can cause irreversible nerve and muscle ischemia. Urgent fasciotomy is the definitive decompressive treatment when indicated, making Option B correct. Observation, tighter compression, or massage can delay or worsen care.
source_original.source_detail: Treatment/Management: acute compartment syndrome is a surgical emergency; remove restrictive dressings/casts and obtain immediate surgical consultation; definitive treatment is urgent fasciotomy when indicated to prevent irreversible nerve and muscle ischemic injury. Current StatPearls/NCBI Bookshelf Acute Compartment Syndrome entry live-rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Physiological Integrity — Physiological Adaptation: acute/complex alterations, emergency response and pathophysiologic adaptation. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Retained the acute-compartment-syndrome construct and key B, upgraded the primary clinical authority to the 2025 AAOS evidence-based CPG, specified an adult client to match that CPG population, and changed the stem to ask for definitive treatment. Replaced implausible distractors with realistic but incomplete/delaying strategies and reduced difficulty from hard to medium because the final item tests a direct emergency-treatment principle.

audit_findings.source_authority: Current AAOS 2025 acute compartment syndrome CPG with NCBI/StatPearls treatment corroboration; NCSBN 2026 for blueprint
audit_findings.currentness: AAOS CPG published/adopted 2025-11-18 and current on AAOS in 2026; StatPearls entry live-rechecked 2026-08-16
audit_findings.exact_locator: AAOS CPG printed pp.10 and 44 > Fasciotomy Methods; StatPearls > Treatment/Management; NCSBN Physiological Adaptation printed p.46 and Medical Emergencies/Pathophysiology content
audit_findings.claim_audit: Final item limits itself to confirmed adult acute compartment syndrome and the directly supported need for urgent fasciotomy/complete decompression. It distinguishes initial cast removal/supportive care from definitive treatment and introduces no unsupported pressure threshold or timing cutoff.

distractor_audit.A: Removal of constriction is appropriate initial management but observation without operative decompression is not definitive treatment for confirmed ACS.
distractor_audit.B: Correct: urgent fasciotomy with complete compartment decompression is the definitive treatment.
distractor_audit.C: Incorrect because elevation above heart level can compromise arterial inflow and delaying decompression is unsafe.
distractor_audit.D: Incorrect because serial examinations are useful during evaluation/risk monitoring, not as sole treatment after confirmed ACS.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: The stem explicitly asks for definitive treatment after confirmation; only B is definitive operative decompression, while A is an initial adjunct.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are plausible management strategies rather than absurd mechanisms; the stem's 'definitive treatment' wording eliminates ambiguity between initial and operative care.
audit_findings.blueprint: Physiological Adaptation — acute/life-threatening conditions, tissue perfusion, complication recognition, and emergency intervention.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Re-audited the current AAOS CPG and rendered fasciotomy recommendation pages, StatPearls treatment section, NCSBN 2026 Physiological Adaptation rendered page, all options, rationale, objective, adult-population scope, ambiguity, cueing, and unsupported precision. B remained uniquely correct.
